newsitem.title: USA: U.S. general defends plan for stealth jet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. general defends plan for stealth jet.

text.p: The Air Force's top general, noting that more than 2,000 U.S. fighter planes were shot down during the Vietnam War, on Tuesday defended plans to develop a dominating new U.S. stealth fighter for 21st century combat.

"We ended up with a rather alarming record" in Vietnam, Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ronald Fogleman told reporters, adding that the proposed radar-avoiding F-22 jet will be needed to control enemy air space in years ahead.

Critics have questioned whether the Pentagon can afford a projected $67 billion for more than 400 of the jets from around 2004 while it also develops a costly new joint strike fighter for the Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps.
But Fogleman said in response to questions that U.S. and allied control of skies over Iraq in the 1991 Gulf War showed that advanced technology was necessary against air defences.

He said the U.S. military did not develop a new and dominating fighter aircraft between the Korean and Vietnam Wars and U.S. planes were vulnerable to ground fire and Soviet-made fighter jets over Vietnam.
"The United States Air Force lost over that 10-year period about 1,500 fighters. The Navy lost 580-some, the Marines lost a couple of hundreds of them," Fogleman told reporters.
"Everybody says we'll never do a Vietnam again. They also say we're never going to do another Desert Storm (Gulf War), we're never going to do another World War II," he added.
"I suspect we will find ways to make the same mistakes that we have made in the past. And so I think we've got to pay attention to these areas."
The general said that there were many "simplistic" arguments against costly new weapons, including the collapse of the Soviet Union which left the United States as the only superpower.
But he said that a "third or fourth-rate" set of air defence threats such as those once used by Vietnam could again challenge U.S. air superiority.
